tagline: Through the Catawba Valley, a mill community between mountain and ridge.
intro: Route 785 follows the Catawba Valley, running as Catawba Road from Lusters Gate to the Roanoke County line and as Blacksburg Road onward to Catawba. At McDonalds Mill, the road lies on the valley floor between Paris Mountain to the south and Gallion Ridge to the north.

George McDonald operated the mill that gave McDonalds Mill its name; its post office served the community from 1847 to 1913. Bennetts Mill also had a country post office, operating from 1876 to 1906, with M. D. Bennett as an early postmaster. The road later became part of U.S. Bicycle Route 76. That bicycle route grew from the Bikecentennial tour organized for the nation’s 1976 bicentennial and became a U.S. Bicycle Route in 1982.

Travel from Lusters Gate toward McDonalds Mill, then continue on Blacksburg Road to Catawba. This section crosses from the Roanoke River watershed into the James River watershed. At Catawba, Route 785 meets Route 311; Route 779 continues along the valley of Catawba Creek.

moments.title: McDonalds Mill
moments.text: Paris Mountain and Gallion Ridge define the setting of McDonalds Mill, a community on Route 785 at the floor of the Catawba Valley. George McDonald operated the mill that supplied its name. The post office used the plural form, McDonalds Mills, during its years of operation from 1847 to 1913.

moments.title: Catawba
moments.text: Catawba Valley is bounded on the south by Catawba Mountain’s northern slope and on the north by mountains along the Craig County border. Farms occupy this rural community beyond Catawba Mountain, where Route 311 meets Routes 785 and 779. Near Route 311, Catawba Hospital traces its history to a resort established in 1857 for the believed healing properties of a sulfur and limestone spring. The Commonwealth of Virginia operates it as a mental health facility. The Appalachian Trail passes through the Catawba area, connecting the landscape with three overlooks: Dragon’s Tooth, McAfee Knob and Tinker Cliffs.

moments.title: McAfee Knob
moments.text: The rock ledge at McAfee Knob projects from Catawba Mountain above a valley 1,600 feet below. This is an Appalachian Trail excursion from Route 311, with a gradual climb ending on exposed rocky terrain. The ridge is covered in pine forest, although much of Catawba Mountain was open farmland in the mid-twentieth century. The name commemorates James McAfee, a Scottish-Irish immigrant who settled in the valley in the late 1730s. From the overlook, North Mountain lies to the west, Tinker Cliffs to the north and the Roanoke Valley to the east.
